query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy to a rapid thermal annealing (RTA) treatment will induce nanoscale atomic ordering (e.g., formation of an L10-type ordered domain) that increases magnetic anisotropy, resulting in a higher coercivity compared to the disordered, soft-ferromagnetic baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with a disordered face‐centered cubic (FCC) structure exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step rapid thermal annealing process at an optimized temperature (e.g., in the 600–800°C range) for a brief period followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: The RTA must be performed under conditions that are sufficient to drive short-range ordering without causing major phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity, so the alloy retains its equiatomic, high-entropy character.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale ordering in the form of L10 (or similarly ordered) domains embedded within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The RTA treatment favors atomic rearrangement over a very short time scale, promoting ordering and the development of high magnetic anisotropy domains. These ordered regions act as pinning sites for domain walls, thereby increasing the material’s coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The RTA-treated alloy is expected to show a significantly increased coercivity relative to the as-deposited, disordered FCC alloy—potentially increasing by at least one order of magnitude, as suggested by analogous behaviors in related HEAs.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy in its as-synthesized, disordered FCC state (such as seen in the FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives with soft ferromagnetism).
generation.boundary: The intervention must be optimized so that the applied temperature and duration are high enough to induce ordering without triggering unwanted phase decomposition. Its effectiveness may be limited if other alloying elements are present in amounts that suppress ordering.
generation.uncertainty: While RTA-induced ordering is anticipated to increase coercivity through enhanced anisotropic pinning, the exact ordering phase and magnitude of coercivity enhancement depend sensitively on the annealing parameters. Further optimization and verification are required.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy samples and split them into two groups. Subject one group to the specified RTA process (e.g., 600–800°C for a controlled duration followed by quenching) and keep the other group as a control. Use X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to detect any ordering (e.g., emergence of L10 peaks or nanoscale ordered domains). Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops to determine the coercivity of both sets of samples.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns (to detect ordered phases)
Transmission electron microscopy images (to resolve nanoscale ordering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated samples show no evidence of atomic ordering (i.e., no additional ordered phase reflections or ordered domains observed) or if their coercivity is not significantly higher than that of the control (disordered) samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe vast high entropy alloy (HEA) composition space is promising for discovery of new material phases with unique properties. This study explores the potential to achieve rare‐earth‐free high magnetic anisotropy materials in single‐phase HEA thin films. Thin films of FeCoNiMnCu sputtered on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature are magnetically soft, with a coercivity on the order of 10 Oe. After post‐deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA), the films exhibit a single face‐centered‐cubic phase, with an almost 40‐fold increase in coercivity. Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase. These results demonstrate a promising HEA approach to achieve high magnetic anisotropy materials using RTA.Keywords: high entropy alloy, magnetic anisotropy, rapid thermal annealing High entropy alloy (HEA) thin films are explored to achieve high magnetic anisotropy phases.
